title: Geometry-only synthetic maps confirmed the zebrafish retina-path wiring advantage at 10 distance strata, not at 20, and showed mouse brain-wide visual reliability does not follow specific retina paths
abstract: Question: campaign studies found that regions farther from the retina in the connectome have less reliable visual responses. Real wiring beat distance-rewired graphs in larval zebrafish (sci:sha256:6e6b5461) but not across the mouse brain (sci:sha256:19f7eb8e). Distance-decile rewiring can be liberal for spatially smooth maps (sci:sha256:f4e4c521), so the species difference could come from the null model. Method: with a plan frozen before analysis, we fitted spatial Gaussian-process models (distance-from-entry trend plus spatial noise; noise only; and a positive control with a real-path effect) to each published region map, drew 1,000 synthetic maps per model, and applied the original rewiring test with 1,000 new rewired graphs. Results: the uncalibrated path-distance tests were only mildly liberal (false-positive rate 2-10% in zebrafish, 4-16% in mouse). In zebrafish (63 regions), real D_ret kept its advantage: calibrated p = 0.038 raw and 0.001 partial (Holm 0.038, 0.001), with five other spatial models p <= 0.024. With 20 distance strata the raw advantage was not significant (p = 0.148; partial p = 0.025); with 50 strata the rewired graphs approached the real graph (rho 0.91) and the test had no power. In mouse, the failed brain-wide test had 74-87% power in 4 of 5 conditions, and the observed advantage was smaller than real-path maps predict (p = 0.004-0.016 in 4 of 5). The exploratory mouse isocortex advantage survived at the margin (calibrated p 0.009-0.029; Holm 0.045-0.054); the hop-count advantage did not (Holm 0.20-0.24). Limitations: stationary isotropic spatial models; model-based power; reanalysis of published region maps; one structural graph per species; 14-65 regions.
